place.en: The Si · Outside the stone door

setup.zh: 三天后，潮水要回来了。你不早不晚，混在人群里出来，空着手，一身泥。「捡到什么了？」「一撮土。」
setup.en: Three days later the tide is coming back. You come out neither early nor late, in the crowd, empty-handed and muddy. "Find anything?" "A pinch of earth."

recap.zh: 你空着手出了秘境；阿禾问你是不是长高了。腊月初七，周衡在告示栏贴出一张纸：外门大比，明日。
recap.en: You came out of the hidden realm empty-handed; Ah He asked if you'd grown. On the seventh of the twelfth month Zhou Heng posted a notice: the outer court contest, tomorrow.

zh: 三天后，秘境关闭。你空着手出来。
告示栏：外门大比，明日。头名，筑基丹一枚。
en: Three days on, the hidden realm closes. You come out empty-handed.
The notice board: the outer court contest, tomorrow. First place, one Foundation pill.

story.zh:
话分两头。那一日小满往左，阿禾往右。

她照着肚子里那张地图走：长廊，第一间石室，第二间石室门口地上第三块石板，踩上去会翻——她站在那块石板旁边，喊了一声「别踩第三块」。一个听了；一个没来得及听，给后头的人一挤，掉了下去，坑里「哎哟」一声，是孙二狗的嗓子。她给人群推着往前走，回头喊了第二声，没有人应。第三间石室，地图上注着「十年前，无」，果然是无；桥那头的灵草园子，她到的时候，最后一株给人连根拔了，两个老弟子为了它在泥里滚成一团。

阿禾没有去抢。她绕开那两个人，顺着干河床往下游走，走了半里，河床边上有一片地，是黑的，黑得发亮，一根草也不长，跟石坳村她家那面坡田，一个样子——她爹说，坡田一年比一年薄，今年又少收了两成，家里添了弟弟，多了一张嘴。黑地的边上，偏偏冒着一株草，三片叶子，紫里透金。阿禾在地图上见过它的样子，旁边注着一行小字：「紫须芝，一株抵三块灵石。」三块灵石，是外门一个月的份例。

她蹲下去，手刚伸到那株草跟前，指头底下的黑土一松，露出半粒东西来，小小的，黑的，硬得像石子。她拈起来凑到眼前，就着光转了一圈，看出来了：是谷，烧焦了一样的谷，还看得出壳上的纹路。她拿指甲再往下抠，又一粒——那片黑地底下，一垄一垄，排得整整齐齐。

很久很久以前，这里有人种过地。

上游那两个老弟子滚完了泥，吵着往这边来了，一个眼尖，已经瞧见了那一点紫。阿禾的手停在那株草和那几粒谷中间。那株紫须芝的根，须子一根一根，正缠在那一垄谷里——拔草，便连根带谷翻成一团烂泥；抠谷，草便是人家的。她低下头，一粒一粒，抠出三粒来。等她抬起头，那株紫须芝已经在一个老弟子的手里，那人冲她一笑：「小师妹，蹲着找什么呢？捡土么？」

她把三粒黑谷包进一小块布里，跟袄襟里缝着的那三十粒禾种挨在一处。地图钱，半块灵石，白花了；一个月的份例，让了。她蹲在黑地边上，掏出小本子记了一笔：**冬月初二。秘境。紫须芝一株，让了。谷，三粒，黑的，不能吃。**记完了，想了想，又添了一行：**有人种过。**

第三天，小满把空玉匣合上，放回石台正中，摆得端端正正；又在那四个空坑旁边蹲下，拿手掌量了一遍：七拃，没错。他对着四个空坑，拱了拱手，说不上为什么，银月也没有问他拱的是谁。

他走出那道墙，墙在身后「轰隆隆」地合上了。崖壁上那一圈青白的光还亮着，六只壁虎还贴在上头，饿得连「呜」都呜不出来了；马小宝嘴里那根萝卜只剩一小截，两颊鼓着，眼睛却还死死瞪着身边那几个跟班。小满从他们底下走过去，走得很轻。走到马小宝底下，头顶上忽然落下一句话来，声音压得极低，低得只有崖底下这一个人听得见：「沈小满。」

小满站住了。马小宝脸贴着石头，只拿眼角往下斜着，一个字一个字地道：「那面墙后头有什么，我不问。」他把嘴里那截萝卜往腮帮子里一顶，「我爹的信到了。腊月里，他亲自坐船来，给我捎丹，还有我家祖上那面镜子——不是我娘给的那面照下巴的，是能照妖的那一面。」他喘了一口气，眼白在青光里一翻，「大比台上，我当着全外门，拿它照一照你。你这三天在墙后头干了什么，照得出来。」

小满没有答话。胸口的木牌，在「照妖」两个字上烫了一下，又烫了一下，一直烫到他爬出那道石缝，还没有凉。

长廊的尽头，离石门只剩几十步，横着一块青石板，一丈见方，前人叫它「称石」。它只称出去的人：进门时一道纹也不亮，出门时，人踩上去，石面上便亮起几道纹：几道纹，便是几层。三百多人要出秘境，只这一条道，谁也绕不过去。石板四周早围了一圈人，踩一个，哄一声：「二层！」「三层——不赖！」「零层，一道都没亮！」有个老弟子踩上去亮了四道，给围着的人抬着出去了，比捡了灵草还风光。

小满挤在人堆后头，手心里全是汗。他如今是五层，一身灵气收得再紧，压不压得住石头，他没把握——一脚踩上去，要是亮出五道纹来，三百多双眼睛，一个也不会看错。他看了看地图，第二间石室门口画着那个翻板坑，坑边一行小字：「坑底有旧水道，通长廊尽头。」他掉头往回走，走到那块第三石板跟前，四下无人，一脚踩了上去。

石板一翻，他掉进了坑里。坑有一丈来深，坑壁滑得像抹了油，坑底果然有一道半人高的旧水道，黑洞洞的，往石门那头去。他正要猫腰钻进去，头顶上一暗，一截剑鞘伸了下来。坑口蹲着一个穿淡蓝衣裳的师姐，面无表情：「又一个。抓着。」

小满不敢不抓。他抓住剑鞘，装着手脚发软，蹬两下，滑一下，蹬两下，又滑一下——可他忘了一样：那剑鞘上，从头到尾没吃着他半分分量。上了坑口，他冲她作了个揖：「多谢师姐。」那师姐低头看了看自己握鞘的手，又看了看他，道：「你没往下坠。」说完，收了剑，往称石那边去了，一脚踩上去，石面上亮了六道纹，四下里一片吸气的声音。

小满望了望那道水道口，又望了望那个淡蓝的背影，到底没有再下去。他把一身的灵气往里收，收了又收，跟着人群挤到称石跟前，一脚踩了上去——石面上亮了一道，又亮了一道，便不亮了。「二层！」有人笑，「五行杂灵根，进去三天，还是二层！」他低着头走了过去，后背上的汗，把灰袍子贴在了身上。那两道纹，是他咬着牙硬压出来的；再多站一口气的工夫，第三道便要亮了。

三天后，潮水要回来了。鲁泥鳅蹲在河滩上，拿一根芦苇插在泥里，看了半天，道：「比上回早了半个时辰。」旁人问他怎么知道，他说他爷爷那回也插过一根，记在门板上，一根比一根早。说完了，他压低嗓子，冲身边几个人道：「马家定了我爹的船，腊月初六，从县城往山脚运东西，定钱都给了。说是舱里要搁一面拿红布包着的镜子，谁也不许揭，揭了赔一条船。」外门弟子一个个从石门里出来，有的捧着一株灵草，捧得像捧着自己的性命；更多的空着手，一身泥，一脸晦气。观主玄沉子还站在石门前，两只手拢在袖子里，像是这三天，他一步也没有挪过。

小满出来得不早也不晚，混在人群里，也是空着手，一身泥。孙二狗早出来了，灰袍从领口撕到了腰，额角肿着一个青包，十个指甲劈了好几个。他双手递过那根萝卜来，完完整整，一口没咬：「沈师兄，还你。」小满道：「你怎么了？」孙二狗道：「掉进翻板坑了。坑壁滑，爬不上来，喊，人都在抢灵草。后来坑口伸下来一截剑鞘，一个穿淡蓝衣裳的师姐，一句话也没说，把我拽了上来，又从怀里掰了半块干粮塞给我，就走了。」他红着脸，「我问她姓什么，她不说。旁边有人叫她秦师姐。……我饿了，吃的是她那半块。萝卜，还你。」小满把他的手推了回去：「你留着。」孙二狗一瘸一拐地走了，那个背影瘦得像一根竹竿，可是走了一路，没有倒。

阿禾蹲在河滩上一块石头旁边，看见他，站起身来，拍了拍身上的泥：「捡到什么了？」小满道：「一撮土。」阿禾道：「……土？」小满道：「土。你呢？」阿禾摊开手心，是一小块布，布里三粒黑东西：「谷。」小满凑过去看了半天：「……烧焦了？」阿禾道：「老了。很老很老。那边河床上的黑土里抠出来的，有人在秘境里头种过地。」她把布包好，揣回袄襟里。他捡的是一撮土，她捡的是三粒死谷——两样都是土里的东西。小满没说话，心里却一动：石室南墙上那个背着筐、往水里撒土的人，撒过的地方，长出了草。

阿禾走了两步，又回过头来，上上下下打量了他一回，道：「你是不是……长高了？」小满后背一紧。他缩了缩脖子，又缩了缩肩膀，把自己往矮里缩了一寸，道：「秘境里冷，缩了三天，一出来，伸开了。」阿禾「哦」了一声，把他从头看到脚，道：「冷的人，缩着才对。」说完转身走了，没有掏本子。小满站在那里，把一身的灵气往里收，收得紧紧的，收成一只漏勺的样子。他心想：从今往后，这一门功夫，比什么都要紧。

石门合上前的最后半个时辰，马小宝他们出来了。五个跟班一个架着一个，饿得两眼发绿；马小宝一身簇新的法衣糊满了泥，嘴里死死衔着一截萝卜缨子，谁多看一眼，他便瞪谁。一个跟班出了石门，腿一软，扑在门边的石壁上便不肯下来了，旁人去拉，他死死扒着石头，嘴里念念叨叨：「……我不是壁虎。我不是壁虎。」大通铺上讲鬼故事的那个老弟子正在人群里，脸都白了：「我说什么来着？疯了一个！」

执事拿着名册迎上去：「你们六个，怎么出来得这般晚？」一个跟班抢着道：「走错了，走到左边那道崖上，碰着了前人的阵，粘了三天。自己碰着的。」没有一个人提沈小满——提了沈小满，便得先说自己爬下那道崖是去做什么的。执事在名册上勾了六个勾。马小宝走过那个抄着手的跟班身边，一口萝卜缨子啐在他脚面上：「报的什么信！」那跟班低着头，没敢吭声，眼睛却往人群后头的小满那边斜了一斜——那一眼里的账，比马小宝的还深。只有石门前那个拢着手的人，听到「左边那道崖」几个字的时候，眼皮动了一动。玄沉子转过头去，望着那道黑洞洞的石门里左边的方向，望了很久；然后把目光收回来，在河滩上三百多个一身泥的弟子里，一个一个看过去。看到小满的时候，停了一停。

只停了一停。他朝小满招了招手。小满心里一沉，走了过去。玄沉子温和地问：「往哪边走的？」小满道：「右边。人多。」玄沉子「嗯」了一声，低头看了看他的草鞋。草鞋帮子上，沾着几点青苔，湿的，绿得发黑——左边那道石阶上长的青苔，右边的长廊是干的，一根草也不长。玄沉子看了一会儿，抬起头来，笑了一笑，道：「右边人多。」说完这一句，便不再看他，接着数他的人了。小满站回人群里。潮水已经漫上来了，漫过淤泥滩，漫过石门的门楣。他低着头，数自己草鞋上的泥点子，数到第十七个，后背上的汗才下去。
story.en:
Meanwhile — that day Xiaoman went left, and A He went right.

She went by the map in her head: the corridor, the first chamber, the third flagstone at the door of the second chamber that tips when you tread on it — she stood beside it and shouted, "Don't step on the third one!" One heard; one didn't hear in time, was shoved by the crowd behind and dropped through, and an "ow!" came up out of the pit in Sun Ergou's voice. The crowd pushed her on; she looked back and shouted again; no one answered. The third chamber, marked "ten years ago, none" on the map, was indeed none; the herb garden past the bridge — when she got there the last plant had been pulled up by the roots, and two seniors were rolling in the mud over it.

A He didn't fight for it. She went round the two of them and followed the dry riverbed downstream, and half a li on, beside it, lay a patch of ground, black, black and shiny, not a blade of grass on it — just like her family's hillside field in Shi'ao Village. Her father said the hillside grew thinner every year; this year it gave two-tenths less again, and there was a baby brother now, one more mouth. At the edge of the black patch, of all places, grew a single plant, three leaves, purple shot with gold. A He had seen it on the map, with a small note beside it: "Purple-whisker zhi, one plant worth three spirit stones." Three stones was a month's outer-court allowance.

She crouched, and just as her hand reached the plant the black earth gave under her fingers and showed half of something, tiny, black, hard as a pebble. She held it close to her eyes, turned it once in the light, and saw what it was: grain, grain as if burnt, the lines of its husk still showing. She dug with a fingernail and found another — under that black patch, row by row, they lay in neat lines.

Long, long ago, someone had farmed here.

The two seniors upstream had finished rolling in the mud and came arguing her way, and one sharp-eyed one had already spotted the dot of purple. A He's hand hung between the plant and the grains. The purple-whisker zhi's roots, whisker by whisker, were wound right through that row of grain — pull the plant, and roots and grain came up together in a mess of mud; dig the grain, and the plant was theirs. She bent her head and dug out three, one by one. When she looked up, the purple-whisker zhi was in a senior's hand, and he grinned at her: "Little sister, what are you crouching there for? Picking up dirt?"

She wrapped the three black grains in a scrap of cloth and put them beside the thirty seed grains sewn into the front of her jacket. The half stone for the map, wasted; a month's allowance, given up. Crouched by the black ground, she wrote in her notebook: **Second of the eleventh month. Hidden realm. Purple-whisker zhi, one, let go. Grain: three, black, not edible.** Then, after a thought, one more line: **Someone farmed here.**

On the third day Xiaoman closed the empty jade box and set it back square in the middle of the altar; then he crouched by the four empty pits and measured once more with his hand: seven spans, right. He cupped his fists to the four pits — he couldn't have said why — and Yinyue didn't ask whom he was saluting.

He went out through the wall, and it rumbled shut behind him. The blue-white ring on the cliff still glowed and the six geckos still hung there, too hungry even to mmf; the radish in Ma Xiaobao's mouth was down to a stub, his cheeks bulging, his eyes glaring at the followers beside him. Xiaoman passed beneath them softly. As he passed under Ma Xiaobao, a voice dropped down to him, pitched so low only the one at the foot of the cliff could hear: "Shen Xiaoman."

Xiaoman stopped. Face to the rock, Ma Xiaobao squinted down and said, word by word: "What's behind that wall, I won't ask." He pushed the stub of radish into his cheek. "My father's letter came. In the twelfth month he's coming by boat himself, bringing me pills, and our family's old mirror — not the one Ma gave me for looking at my chin; the one that shows demons." He panted; the whites of his eyes rolled in the blue light. "On the contest stage, in front of the whole outer court, I'll hold it up to you. Whatever you did behind that wall these three days — it'll show."

Xiaoman didn't answer. At the word demons the token on his chest went hot, then hot again, and it was still hot when he had climbed out through the crack.

At the end of the long corridor, only a few dozen steps from the stone door, lay a bluestone slab ten feet square that the old ones called the Weighing Stone. It weighed only those going out: coming in, not a line lit; going out, step on it and lines lit up on its face — so many lines, so many layers. Three hundred-odd people had to leave the realm, and this was the only way; no one could go round. A ring of people had gathered, and at each one who stepped on it a roar went up: "Layer two!" "Three — not bad!" "Layer zero, not a single line!" One senior lit four lines and was carried out on the crowd's shoulders, prouder than if he'd found an herb.

Xiaoman, squeezed in at the back, had sweat in his palms. He was at layer five now; however tightly he drew his qi in, whether he could hold it down against the stone he wasn't sure — one step, and if five lines lit, not one of three hundred pairs of eyes would misread it. He looked at the map: at the door of the second chamber was the tipping-slab pit, and beside it a note: "Old drain at the pit's bottom, runs to the end of the corridor." He turned back, went to the third flagstone, and with no one about, stepped on it.

The slab tipped and he dropped into the pit. It was ten feet deep, its walls slick as if oiled, and at the bottom, sure enough, was an old drain half a man high, black, running toward the stone door. He was about to stoop into it when the light above went dim and a scabbard came down. At the lip crouched a senior sister in pale blue, expressionless: "Another one. Grab hold."

Xiaoman didn't dare not grab. He took the scabbard and made a show of weak arms and legs, kick twice, slip once, kick twice, slip again — but he forgot one thing: from first to last, the scabbard never took half an ounce of his weight. At the lip he bowed to her: "Thank you, sister." She looked down at the hand that held the scabbard, then at him: "You didn't hang." And she sheathed her sword and went to the Weighing Stone, stepped on it, and six lines lit on its face, and a gasp went round.

Xiaoman looked at the drain's mouth, then at that pale-blue back, and in the end didn't go down again. He drew his qi in, and in again, followed the crowd to the Weighing Stone and stepped on — one line lit, then another, and no more. "Layer two!" someone laughed. "Five-element mixed roots, three days inside, still layer two!" He walked across with his head down, his grey robe stuck to his back with sweat. Those two lines he had forced down with his teeth clenched; a breath longer on the stone and the third would have lit.

Three days later the tide was coming back. Lu the Loach crouched on the flats, pushed a reed into the mud, studied it a good while and said: "Half an hour earlier than last time." Asked how he knew, he said his grandfather had pushed in a reed last time too and marked it on the door plank, each one earlier than the last. Then he lowered his voice to the few beside him: "The Ma family's hired my father's boat — sixth of the twelfth month, cargo from the county town to the foot of the mountain, deposit paid. They say there'll be a mirror wrapped in red cloth in the hold, and nobody's to unwrap it — unwrap it and you pay for the boat." The outer disciples came out of the stone door one by one: some holding an herb as if holding their own lives; more empty-handed, muddy, glum. Abbot Xuanchenzi still stood before the door with his hands in his sleeves, as if he hadn't moved a step in three days.

Xiaoman came out neither early nor late, lost in the crowd, empty-handed too, muddy. Sun Ergou was out already, his robe torn from collar to waist, a blue lump on his brow, several fingernails split. He held out the radish in both hands, whole, not one bite gone: "Brother Shen, here, it's yours." "What happened to you?" "Fell into the tipping-slab pit. The walls were slick, I couldn't climb out; I shouted, but everyone was fighting over herbs. Then a scabbard came down over the edge — a senior sister in pale blue, and she didn't say a word, just hauled me up, broke off half her ration and pushed it at me, and went." He went red. "I asked her name; she wouldn't say. Somebody near called her Sister Qin. …When I got hungry I ate her half. The radish — it's yours." Xiaoman pushed his hands back: "Keep it." Sun Ergou limped off, his back thin as a bamboo pole — and it went the whole way without falling.

A He was crouching by a rock on the flats; seeing him she stood and brushed off the mud. "Find anything?" "A pinch of earth." "…Earth?" "Earth. You?" She opened her hand: a scrap of cloth, three black things in it. "Grain." Xiaoman peered at it a long time. "…Burnt?" "Old. Very, very old. Dug out of the black earth by the riverbed over there. Someone farmed inside the hidden realm." She wrapped it up and put it back in her jacket. He had found a pinch of earth, she three dead grains — both things of the soil. Xiaoman said nothing, but something stirred in him: the man on the chamber's south wall with the basket on his back, scattering earth into the water — where he scattered, grass grew.

A He took two steps, turned back and looked him up and down. "Have you… grown?" Xiaoman's back went tight. He hunched his neck, hunched his shoulders, shrank himself an inch: "It was cold in there. I was hunched up three days, and when I came out I stretched." "Oh," said A He, and looked him over from head to foot. "People who are cold ought to stay hunched." She turned and went, and didn't take out her notebook. Xiaoman stood there drawing his qi in, tight, tight, into the shape of a skimmer. From now on, he thought, this one skill matters more than anything.

In the last half hour before the stone door shut, Ma Xiaobao's lot came out. The five followers held each other up, eyes green with hunger; Ma Xiaobao, his brand-new robe caked in mud, clamped a stub of radish greens in his teeth and glared at anyone who looked. One follower, out of the door, went weak at the knees, flopped against the rock by the door and wouldn't come off it; when they pulled at him he clung to the stone muttering, "…I'm not a gecko. I'm not a gecko." The senior who'd told ghost stories in the long bunk was in the crowd and went white: "What did I tell you? One went mad!"

The steward went to meet them with the register. "You six — why so late?" A follower got in first: "Took a wrong turn, ended up on the left cliff, hit some old binding, stuck three days. Hit it ourselves." Not one of them mentioned Shen Xiaoman — mention him, and first they'd have to say what they'd climbed down that cliff for. The steward ticked six names. Passing the follower with folded arms, Ma Xiaobao spat a mouthful of radish greens on his foot: "Some message you brought!" The man kept his head down and said nothing, but his eyes slid sideways toward Xiaoman at the back of the crowd — and the account in that look ran deeper than Ma Xiaobao's. Only the man with his hands in his sleeves before the door, at the words the left cliff, let his eyelids flicker. Xuanchenzi turned and looked a long time into the black doorway, toward the left; then drew his gaze back and ran it over the three hundred muddy disciples on the flats one by one. At Xiaoman it paused.

Paused only. He beckoned. Xiaoman's heart sank; he went over. Xuanchenzi asked mildly, "Which way did you go?" "Right. More people." "Mm." The abbot looked down at his straw sandals. On their sides clung a few flecks of moss, wet, green going on black — the moss of the steps on the left; the corridor on the right was dry, not a blade of anything. Xuanchenzi looked a while, then raised his head, smiled, and said: "More people on the right." And with that he didn't look at him again, and went on counting his people. Xiaoman went back into the crowd. The tide was already coming over the flats, over the lintel of the stone door. Head down, he counted the mud spots on his sandals; at the seventeenth, the sweat on his back finally dried.

label.en: Enough for today — the contest is tomorrow

story.zh:
小满去执事房领小狰。周衡正低着头打算盘，小狰趴在账簿上，睡得四脚朝天，肚子鼓得像一只小西瓜，尾巴盖住了他要翻的那一页；周衡的手停在半空，没有去翻。见他进来，周衡把一张纸推了过来：**冬月初一，萝卜三根。初二，五根。初三，三根。执事房窗纸一张（咬破）。账簿一页（啃了一角）。**小满道：「……周师兄，账簿那一角，也要算？」周衡道：「账簿的角，也是账。照规矩，灵兽的开销，记在主人名下。」

小满道：「我没钱。」周衡道：「我知道。」小满想了一想，一脸诚恳：「周师兄，公中那边，马师兄说过，畜生也要吃饭——所以我初一交了两块。这十一根萝卜，是不是该从公中里出？」周衡拨算盘的手停住了，看着他，嘴角动了一动，动得极轻，轻得像账簿上一粒没掸干净的灰。他提起笔，在那张纸的最底下添了一行：**公中代付。**写完了，又翻开巡夜簿，在十月那一页底下添了一行小字：**上旬丢十株。巡夜至今，一株未失。另议。**小满问：「另议什么？」周衡道：「腊八结账。」

那天夜里，大通铺上三天没睡安稳的人，一沾铺便打起了鼾。小满悄悄爬起来，把小狰揣进怀里，往柴房去。路过正殿后头，他站住了：殿里点着一盏灯笼。

他从门缝里看进去。空荡荡的大殿，正中那口空石座，灯笼搁在地上，观主玄沉子跪在石座跟前，没有打坐，也没有念经，张着一只手，拇指抵着石面正中那块颜色深些的四方印子，一拃一拃地量过去。量完一边，又量一边。量完了，他跪在那里，半天没动，轻轻道了一句：「……不在那里了。」

小满怀里的小狰，偏偏在这时候打了个喷嚏。玄沉子抬起头来。小满往廊柱后头一缩，摸出一颗石子，往殿门另一头的台阶上一弹，「嗒、嗒」滚了下去。玄沉子提起灯笼，往那头去看了。小满闪身进殿，蹲到石座跟前，张开手掌，拇指抵着那块印子的边，一拃，两拃……七拃。另一边，也是七拃。

七拃。跟石室里那四个空坑，一般大。他蹲在那里，后背一阵发凉：祖师给它留了一口石座，留了三百年，它一天也没有在这石座上站过。它在石室里站过。殿门外头，灯笼的光又晃回来了，他一猫腰，从后门溜了出去。

到了柴房后头，月亮很亮。他盘腿坐下，从怀里摸出那一块灵石——冬月初一剩下的那一块，秘境里没舍得用——握在手心，吸了一口。只一口。那块灵石在他手心里先是一凉，跟着一暗，灰了；他手指一捏，它成了一把粉，从指缝里漏了下去。

小满愣愣地看着那把粉。从前是漏勺，一块灵石，他要吸上小半个月；如今是水缸，一口。水缸是装得多了，可水缸也吃水，吃得更凶。他在心里算：一个月三块，交公中两块，剩一块，一口；离腊月初八，还有三十五天。他溜进柴房，把那只小铜炉从柴垛底下掏出来，把那一把粉倒进炉口里试了试。炉盖「咔哒」一声合上，隔了一会儿，又「咔哒」一声弹开，那把粉原样吐了出来，吐了他一手。饭桶炼得出九转的丹，可它只尝过回春丹，只会炼回春丹；回春丹治伤；那一回的余劲推过他一层，再往上，推不动了——灵石的灰，它不吃。马小宝那里，腊月里马家的船就要到了，船上是丹，还有一面拿红布包着的镜子。他低头看了看胸口的木牌，头一回觉得，这块木头贴在心口，是烫手的。

他小声道：「银月。」木牌没有回答。他又小声道：「……今天那个故事，你还没讲完。那个禹，铸了九口鼎，一州一口，后来呢？」木牌还是没有回答。他等了很久，以为她睡着了，正要站起身来，一个很轻很轻的声音，在他耳朵里响了一下，轻得他差点以为是风：「……后来，沉了。」

他站在月光底下，一动也不动。柴房外头，远远的，是泗水的声音。潮水涨满了，那条讲理的河，在黑地里一下一下地拍着岸，拍得很慢，很匀，像是有人在河底下，隔着一层水，在慢慢地呼吸。

腊月初七一早，周衡在外门的告示栏上贴了一张纸，纸上写着：**外门大比，明日。头名，筑基丹一枚。**
story.en:
Xiaoman went to the stewards' office to fetch the little zheng. Zhou Heng was bent over his abacus; the zheng lay on the ledger asleep with all four paws in the air, belly round as a small melon, its tails covering the page he wanted to turn; his hand hung in the air and didn't turn it. When Xiaoman came in, Zhou Heng pushed a sheet across: **First of the eleventh month: radishes, three. Second: five. Third: three. Office window paper: one sheet (bitten through). Ledger: one page (corner chewed).** "…Brother Zhou, even the corner of the ledger?" "A ledger's corner is an account too. By the rules, a spirit beast's costs go under its master's name."

"I've no money." "I know." Xiaoman thought, then said with an honest face: "Brother Zhou, over at the common fund, Brother Ma said beasts have to eat too — that's why I paid two on the first. These eleven radishes — shouldn't they come out of the common fund?" Zhou Heng's hand stopped on the abacus. He looked at him, and the corner of his mouth moved — very slightly, slight as a speck of dust not quite brushed off a ledger. He took up his brush and added one line at the bottom: **Paid by the common fund.** Then he opened the night-watch book and added a small line under the tenth month: **Ten lost in the first ten days. Since the watch began, not one lost. To be settled.** "Settled how?" asked Xiaoman. "Accounts close on Laba," said Zhou Heng.

That night everyone on the long bunk, three nights without proper sleep, snored the moment they lay down. Xiaoman crept out with the zheng in his coat, heading for the woodshed. Passing behind the main hall, he stopped: a lantern was lit inside.

He looked in through the crack of the door. The great empty hall, the empty stone plinth in the middle, a lantern on the floor, and Abbot Xuanchenzi kneeling before the plinth — not sitting in meditation, not chanting — one hand spread, his thumb on the edge of the darker square mark in the middle of the stone, spanning it hand over hand. One side, then another. When he'd done he stayed kneeling a long while, and said softly: "…It isn't there any more."

Just then the zheng in Xiaoman's coat sneezed. Xuanchenzi looked up. Xiaoman shrank behind a pillar, fished out a pebble and flicked it onto the steps at the far end of the hall — tick, tick, it rolled down. Xuanchenzi took up the lantern and went to look. Xiaoman slipped in, crouched at the plinth, spread his hand, thumb on the edge of the mark: one span, two… seven. The other side, seven too.

Seven spans. The same as the four empty pits in the chamber. Crouched there, he felt a chill run down his back: the founder had kept a plinth for it three hundred years, and it had never stood on this plinth a single day. It had stood in the chamber. Outside the door the lantern light swung back; he ducked and slipped out the back.

Behind the woodshed the moon was bright. He sat cross-legged and took out his one stone — the one left from the first of the month, which he hadn't used in the realm — held it in his palm and drew one breath. Just one. The stone went cold in his hand, then dark, then grey; he pinched it, and it was a handful of powder running out between his fingers.

Xiaoman stared at the powder. As a skimmer, one stone lasted him half a month; as a water vat, one breath. A vat holds more — but a vat drinks, and drinks harder. He reckoned: three stones a month, two to the common fund, one left, one breath; thirty-five days to the eighth of the twelfth month. He slipped into the woodshed, dug the little bronze furnace out from under the woodpile and tipped the powder into its mouth to see. The lid clicked shut; a moment later it clicked open again and spat the powder back out all over his hand. The rice-bucket could make nine-turn pills, but it had only tasted the healing pill, so it only knew the healing pill; healing pills mend wounds; that one batch's leftover force had pushed him up a layer, but further up it wouldn't push — and stone ash it wouldn't eat. Over at Ma Xiaobao's, the Ma family's boat would come in the twelfth month, with pills aboard, and a mirror wrapped in red cloth. He looked down at the token on his chest, and for the first time that piece of wood against his heart felt too hot to hold.

"Yinyue," he whispered. No answer. "…That story today — you didn't finish it. Yu cast nine cauldrons, one for each province, and then what?" Still no answer. He waited a long time, thought she was asleep, and was about to get up when a very, very faint voice sounded once in his ear, so faint he almost took it for the wind: "…Then they sank."

He stood in the moonlight and didn't move. Beyond the woodshed, far off, was the sound of the Si. The tide was full, and that reasonable river lapped the bank in the dark, stroke after stroke, very slow, very even, as if someone at the bottom of the river, under a layer of water, were slowly breathing.

Early on the seventh of the twelfth month, Zhou Heng pasted a sheet on the outer court's notice board. It read: **Outer court contest: tomorrow. First place: one Foundation pill.**
